items.description: Realpage Economy Express Episode 75 by Arben Skivjani Posted November 13, 2026 in Insights A surprisingly strong jobs report and stubborn inflation have all but settled the Fed's December decision, even as households and homebuyers keep feeling the squeeze. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the October jobs report showed 165,000 new jobs, almost three times what forecasters expected. Unemployment slipped to 4.1%, and paychecks grew 0.4% in a single month, the fastest pace since January. Job openings climbed to 7.5 million in September, more than expected, even though hiring remains slow. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October and core prices were up 0.3% for the third month in a row, while the annual inflation rate could not be published because prices were never collected during last year's shutdown. Producer prices rose a calmer 0.3% in October after September's jump, but they are still up 6.5% from a year ago, the most since 2022. Fed funds futures pricing now treats a December rate hike as a sure thing, with some traders even betting on a half-point move. The University of Michigan's consumer survey found sentiment rose to 51, the best reading since August, while expected inflation eased to about 4.3%. Federal Reserve data show credit card balances grew in September at their fastest pace in nearly three years. Per the National Association of Realtors, existing home sales fell to their slowest pace since 2010, even with more homes for sale than at any point since 2019. For more information on the state of the U.S. Economy, including forecasts, watch all the episodes of the Economy Express series. items.title: Renewals Carry Apartment REIT Pricing as Coastal and Sun Belt Results Split
items.description: Renewals Carry Apartment REIT Pricing as Coastal and Sun Belt Results Split by Meggan Taylor Posted November 12, 2026 in REIT Renewals and low turnover continued to support apartment REIT pricing in 3rd quarter 2026, while new lease performance remained pressured across much of the Sun Belt. Results from Camden Property Trust, Essex Property Trust, Mid-America Apartment Communities (MAA), UDR and Vivmark Residential highlighted a sharp divide between coastal and Sun Belt markets, as coastal-heavy operators raised guidance and Sun Belt-focused peers lowered expectations. A merger and major portfolio shifts reshaped the group Vivmark Residential reported its first quarterly results since AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential completed their merger on Aug. 17, creating a same-store portfolio of 157,377 apartment homes. The company raised its target for yearly cost savings and revenue gains from the combination by $10 million to $135 million. COO Michael Manelis said years of separate operations gave Vivmark “a multi-year A/B test,” letting it compare the two companies’ practices and keep what works best. Other operators also changed their portfolio exposure. Camden completed the roughly $1.6 billion sale of 11 California communities on July 29, and UDR formed a $2 billion partnership with Apollo, covering 19 communities. As a result, three of the five REITs now operate meaningfully different portfolios than a year ago. Renewals continued to carry lease pricing Renewals remained the primary source of pricing strength. Renewal lease rates rose 5.3% at Essex, MAA and Vivmark and 3.6% at Camden, while retention remained elevated across portfolios. UDR reported a record-high 3rd quarter retention rate of 52%, and MAA recorded a record-low share (10.1%) of move-outs to homeownership. Management tied that stability largely to housing costs. “We see sustained high homeownership costs, and we see residents continuing to stay in place, both for cyclical and structural reasons,” UDR CFO Dave Bragg said. MAA added that the dollar gap between new and renewal rents has held at about $190 to $200 for four quarters, a small difference next to the cost and hassle of moving. New lease pricing stayed negative as concessions persisted New lease pricing told a different story. New lease rates declined at four of the five REITs, ranging from -6.0% at MAA to -0.2% at Essex. Vivmark was the only exception, with new lease rates up 0.4%. Camden and MAA attributed the weakness largely to lease-up discounting and lease mix. “Concessions have remained remarkably sticky, seemingly led by many merchant builders now turned reluctant operators,” Camden CEO Alex Jessett said. MAA said its year-to-date new lease decline narrows to -1.9% when the departing resident stayed only one lease term, a figure it views as a better gauge of market rents. Northern California and Denver marked the extremes Regional performance diverged sharply. Northern California led results at both Vivmark and Essex, where same-store NOI rose 11.2% and 7.0%, respectively. At UDR, new lease rates rose 5.7% in the West region but fell 7.2% in the Southwest region. Denver sat at the other end, with same-store NOI down 9.6% at Vivmark and nearly 7% at both Camden and MAA. Essex linked Northern California’s strength to limited supply and rents that remain below historical norms relative to incomes. By its estimate, rents could rise more than 20%, assuming no wage growth, before rent-to-income ratios returned to pre-COVID levels. Meanwhile, Camden tied most of its Denver revenue decline to local legislation that stopped it from billing residents for common-area utilities, on top of persistent concessions. Guidance split along portfolio lines Full-year outlooks followed the same divide. Essex, UDR and Vivmark raised same-store revenue guidance, while Camden and MAA lowered theirs. Both Sun Belt-focused REITs cited timing: MAA said new lease pricing is recovering later than expected, and Camden said September was softer than expected. Both still pointed to early improvement as supply eases. “October new resident lease pricing improved from September, counter to the normal seasonal pattern,” MAA CEO Brad Hill said. What to watch in 4th quarter The key question for 4th quarter is whether easing supply translates into firmer revenue growth in Sun Belt markets. With completions declining and demand holding up, those results should show whether supply-heavy markets are beginning to close the gap with coastal markets. items.title: Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here's why
items.description: Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act 's institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels. According to the National Apartment Association ’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse , released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction , the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out. The industry's legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects. Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry. “I would say it hasn't normalized. In other words, it wasn't where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences , said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD . “I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.” Uncertainty is still taking a toll Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position. “Capital's coming in, but it's not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it's really hard for them to write checks. According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group , a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets. Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere. “When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn't have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview. Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29. "Capital's just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market's still trying to find itself,” Tanner said. In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern. “Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned. The uncertainty surrounding Treasury’s proposed rulemaking The U.S. Department of the Treasury , which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations. “If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, 'all right, built-to-rent is carved out.' But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said. Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy. Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued. The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects. Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban. items.description: Hottest outdoor storage property markets The numbers help explain the appetite. Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses. Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically. The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren't uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial. Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah's IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah's container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025. Petrillo said that there is still plenty of room left for values to increase, so an investor jumping in now hasn't missed the game. "We are still in the very early innings," Petrillo said. Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots. "It comes down to supply and demand," he said. "If you need a warehouse you can usually find one. Properly zoned infill IOS sites are much harder to find and every year more of them are converted to warehouses and other uses," he said, referencing multifamily housing units. The scarcity makes tenants sticky. "So a limited supply keeps shrinking. And because so much of the value is in the land itself, owners keep the option to redevelop the site as the area grows," Cheema added. Because of the imbalance of supply and demand, rents and prices are rising across the board, according to Cheema, but no two IOS properties look alike, which has kept the door open for smaller investors. "Big institutions want exposure to IOS, but ownership is fragmented across mom-and-pop owners and small businesses, so it's hard to deploy large amounts of capital without first aggregating these assets into portfolios," Cheema said. Unlike traditional warehouses, there's no standard spec like square footage or clear height to compare them. "That lack of standardization along with the ongoing growth of the asset class, means there's still runway for small investors to find opportunities," Cheema said. "Financing has improved as more lenders have a better understanding of IOS, but it's still largely local and regional banks," Cheema added. Zoning is the biggest challenge. "If you don't understand the city's plans for the area, you may end up owning a use they're trying to phase out," Cheema said. CanTex Capital works with the city and neighborhoods before buying to ensure the impact aligns with the community's plan for its future. Advantages over traditional industrial, multifamily real estate Alex Sutterer, an executive vice president at NAI Hiffman, a Chicago-area commercial real estate firm, said that beyond being a place to store big equipment, IOS attracts investors for two main reasons: lower capital expenditure requirements than traditional industrial or multifamily properties and the potential for higher yields. "Capital improvements are also less specific to individual tenants, so owners can direct spending toward the property's overall functionality," Sutterer said. For private investors, IOS typically trades at a yield around one percentage point higher than traditional industrial properties, helping attract smaller investors and family offices. "We believe that gap will continue to narrow as more institutional capital enters this space," Sutterer added. Even for industrial properties with similar yields, he said the credit profile of tenants is generally stronger for IOS. Shallow-bay, multitenant industrial properties — industrial facilities that tend to be much smaller than big-box distribution warehouses — have comparable yields. But unlike the local businesses that tend to fill up shallow-bay sites, IOS tenants range from local businesses to those with investment-grade credit ratings, offering investors the potential for both yield and creditworthy tenants. And institutional money is making IOS more competitive. "Institutional capital has increased competition in IOS, and property values and lease rates have risen overall," Sutterer said. He added smaller investors can still find opportunities below institutional deal-size thresholds, although that does not mean every smaller deal is priced fairly. "We see opportunities to add value and earn yield in deals below $3 million–$5 million," Sutterer said. items.title: Building Material Price Inflation Remains High Despite Energy Price Declines
items.description: Building Material Price Inflation Remains High Despite Energy Price Declines November 13, 2026 Jesse Wade No Comments The Producer Price Index for final demand was up 0.3% in October, after rising 1.4% in September. Compared to a year ago, final demand prices were up 6.5%. The price of goods used in new residential construction (including energy) was unchanged over the month and up 9.8% from last year, while the price of services was up 0.7% over the month and up 11.3% from last year. Combining goods and services, the price index for inputs to new residential construction was up 0.3% in October and 10.4% higher than last year. Input Goods The goods component has a larger importance to the inputs to residential construction price index, representing around 60% of the total. On a monthly basis, the price of input goods to new residential construction was unchanged in October after rising 1.7% in September. The input goods to residential construction index can be further broken down into two separate components, one measuring energy inputs with the other measuring remaining goods. The latter of these two components simply represents building materials used in residential construction, which makes up around 93% of the goods index. Energy input prices fell 3.3% in October and were 64.8% higher than a year ago. Building material prices were up 0.5% in October and up 5.8% compared to one year ago. Energy prices fell monthly as No. 2 diesel fuel prices fell 4.6% over the month but was a substantial 115.2% higher than a year ago. Outside of energy products, particleboard and fiberboard prices rose 5.4% over the month and were up 13.9% from a year ago. Softwood veneer and plywood prices were up 3.6% over the month and 24.5% higher than a year ago. Input Services Prices for service inputs to residential construction rose 0.7% in October. On a year-over-year basis, service input prices were up 11.3%. The price index for service inputs to residential construction can be broken out into three separate components: a trade services component, a transportation and warehousing services component, and a services excluding trade, transportation, and warehousing component (other services). The most significant component is trade services (around 60%), followed by other services (around 29%), and finally transportation and warehousing services (around 11%). The largest component, trade services, was up 13.2% from a year ago. The price of transportation and warehousing services has risen 24.6% from a year ago, while prices for other services were up 3.0% over the year. items.title: SpaceX Unveils $74B Data Center Plans In Texas, Arizona
items.description: SpaceX plans to spend $74B developing a pair of large-scale data center campuses in Arizona and Texas, marking a significant expansion of the Elon Musk -owned company’s digital infrastructure footprint. Wikimedia Commons/Gage Skidmore Elon Musk at a memorial service for slain conservative commentator Charlie Kirk The company announced the plans Thursday, outlining a $50B project at a new site in Cochise County, Arizona, and a $24B development on 444 acres near the firm’s headquarters in Starbase, Texas. The two campuses are taking different approaches to power. The Texas facility is planned to be powered by a natural gas power plant that SpaceX itself would develop, own and operate, Bloomberg reported . The Arizona campus, by contrast, would rely at least in part on gird electricity from local cooperatives. SpaceX has said the project will utilize existing renewable resources and cooling systems designed to avoid consuming groundwater — one of the most controversial elements of data center development in the desert Southwest. While SpaceX has been known as a commercial spaceflight company, Musk has increasingly repositioned the firm as an AI infrastructure provider for its own Grok models and outside hyperscale customers. The centerpiece of that shift was SpaceX’s February acquisition of Musk’s xAI in a $1.25T all-stock deal, merging the AI lab’s computing infrastructure into SpaceX’s launch and satellite business. SpaceX’s existing computing infrastructure is almost entirely concentrated in the Memphis, Tennessee, area at a pair of campuses called Colossus I and Colossus 2. The gigawatt-scale cluster has become a focal point for controversy , with environmental and civil rights groups alleging the company operated gas-powered generators to power its data centers without obtaining required Federal permits. Subsequent lawsuits from the NAACP and the Southern Environmental Law Center were opposed by the Trump administration, with the Justice Department asking a judge to dismiss the litigation on national security grounds. While Musk’s data center projects have courted controversy before, the timing of this week’s announcement is notable. It comes just over a week after voters across the U.S. delivered a sharp rebuke of data center development in numerous state and local elections in the industry’s most important markets. At the center of this shift was Texas, which has emerged as the country’s fastest-growing data center hub. Democrats scored upset victories across the state after campaigning in part on tighter oversight of data center development. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott after making more restrictive data center policies a centerpiece of her campaign. The political shift occurred despite Musk reportedly spending roughly $180M supporting Republican candidates in Texas, including a $5M contribution to Abbott’s campaign. In the immediate aftermath of the election, Musk made clear that data center development was among the issues on his mind. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote in a post on X. Arizona also faces the potential for more restrictive regulations on data centers following the midterms. Democrats claimed control over both chambers of the state legislature and retained the governor's office, with legislative Democrats openly discussing a potential pause on new data center development. Gov. Katie Hobbs , however, has said she is opposed to a blanket data center moratorium. Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Elon Musk , SpaceX

items.title: No Relief: Credit Conditions for Builders Still Tightening
items.description: No Relief: Credit Conditions for Builders Still Tightening November 13, 2026 Paul Emrath No Comments Credit conditions on loans for residential Land Acquisition, Development & Construction (AD&C) were still tightening in the third quarter of 2026, according to NAHB’s quarterly survey on AD&C Financing. The net easing index derived from the survey posted a third-quarter reading of -15.3 (the negative number indicating net tightening). This marks the nineteenth consecutive quarter during which residential builders and developers have reported tightening credit conditions. The NAHB survey agrees closely with the third-quarter results reported by lenders in the Federal Reserve’s survey of senior loan officers, as the net easing index constructed from the Fed survey posted a third-quarter reading of -15.5. Although lenders previously reported a slight easing in 2026 Q2, lenders have generally agreed with builders and developers that credit conditions have been tightening since the beginning of 2022. The Fed survey’s net easing index was in negative territory (indicating net tightening) for 18 of the past 19 quarters. More details from the Fed’s survey of lenders—including measures of demand and net easing for residential mortgages—appeared in a previous post . Meanwhile, measures on the cost of AD&C credit exhibited a combination of relatively small quarter-to-quarter changes, signaling no clear trend in either direction. The average contract interest rate declined from 8.09% in the second quarter to 7.83% in the third quarter on loans for land development, but increased for the other three categories of loans tracked in the NAHB AD&C survey: from 7.77% to 8.08% on loans for land acquisition, from 7.28% to 7.72% on loans for speculative single-family construction, and from 7.01% to 7.27% on loans for pre-sold single-family construction. However, the initial points charged by lenders declined on all four categories of AD&C loans in the third quarter: from 1.05% to 0.86% on loans for land acquisition, from 1.05% to 0.97% on loans for land development, from 0.85% to 0.71% on loans for speculative single-family construction, and from 0.71% to 0.51% on loans for pre-sold single-family construction. Those changes left the average effective interest rate (taking both contract rate and initial points into account) essentially unchanged at 11.83% (compared 11.82% in the second quarter) on loans for speculative single-family construction. The average effective rate increased from 10.43% to 10.55% on loans for land acquisition, but declined from 12.59% to 11.69% on loans for land development, and from 11.67% to 11.47% on loans for pre-sold single-family construction. The NAHB AD&C survey also revealed that 32% of respondents who built single-family homes during the third quarter of 2026 financed some of their homes with a construction-to-permanent (one-time-close) loan made to the ultimate home buyer. On average, 58% of the homes these respondents built were financed in this manner. While the market for residential mortgages has been showing signs of stress recently—including a recent decline in mortgage applications and increase in delinquencies —it is important not to overlook the role access to AD&C credit plays in helping builders and developers expand the supply of affordable housing. More detail on credit conditions for residential builders and developers is available on NAHB’s AD&C Financing Survey web page . items.title: Apartment rents diverge: San Francisco rises, the Sun Belt falls
items.description: America's apartment landscape has become a tale of two opposing rent trends. Rents are climbing in the Bay Area and the Midwest, while much of the Sun Belt is still sliding. National same-store asking rents edged up 1.7% from a year earlier in October, the biggest annual gain since May 2023, apartment industry data firm RealPage reported Nov. 11. The national figure hides a wide gap. San Francisco rents jumped 14.7%, evidence of why city officials are pressing the supply button to drive housing construction. San Antonio rents dropped 2.6%. The month-over-month picture illustrates less dramatic change. RealPage showed that rents fell 0.7% in October, the first monthly cut of 2026. The company said the annual gain came less from strong pricing than from weak months dropping out of the calculation, making for stronger year-over-year comparables. Other trackers show the same upward drift, with different monthly readings. Yardi Matrix reported rents up 0.1% in October, with annual growth of 1.4%, the strongest in more than three years. Apartments.com put annual growth at 1.6%, even as rents slipped 0.15% for the month. Supply wave cools Supply and demand are edging toward balance. RealPage said renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year ending in Q3 2026. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units over the same period, almost half the late-2024 peak. Occupancy eased to 95%, down 20 basis points from September. It is still up 40 basis points this year and 10 basis points above October 2025. Landlords hit the brakes Improving rents haven't translated into a property buying spree. Camden Property Trust , a large apartment landlord, walked away from two acquisitions and canceled two planned development projects. The Federal Reserve's rate hike was a main reason, rental economist Jay Parsons wrote on LinkedIn. Two deals under contract fell through after the hike, Camden CEO Alex Jessett said on the third-quarter earnings call. Camden asked for lower prices, and the sellers declined. Buying also beat building on cost. Camden bought an asset at about $370,000 a door, while building it would have cost north of $600,000, Jessett said. Camden's earnings show an unevenly improving market. Funds from operations, a standard earnings measure for real estate investment trusts, were $1.70 per diluted share in the third quarter. Core funds from operations were $1.71, $0.02 above the company's guidance midpoint. "A higher-for-longer rate environment may equate to a lower-for-longer supply environment," Parsons wrote. Fewer projects penciling out means fewer new apartment options for renters. Coasts and Midwest lead Northern California took the top three spots for rent power among the 50 largest markets, RealPage said. San Francisco rose 14.7%, San Jose 9.5% and Oakland 8.5%. All three are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest metros fill much of the rest of the top 10. Milwaukee led at 4.2%, followed by Chicago at 3.3%, and Kansas City and Cleveland at 3.1% each. Detroit and St. Louis each gained 2.7% and just missed the cut. Sun Belt still lags Most Sun Belt and Florida markets continued to decline. The South as a region returned to annual growth, but only by 0.5%. San Antonio had the deepest decline in rents among big markets at 2.6%. Its occupancy of 92.5% was the lowest of the 50 largest markets. Houston fell 1.8%, followed by drops in Tampa of 1%, Charlotte of 0.9% and Denver of 0.8%. Several Sun Belt markets have turned the corner, however. Jacksonville rose 2.6%, Raleigh 1.0%, Atlanta 0.8%, Austin and Miami 0.6% each, and Phoenix 0.4%. items.title: Members Of Congress Have Questions For Brookfield After Its Mass Mobile Home Purchase
items.description: Brookfield quietly closed on the acquisition of the largest privately held manufactured housing portfolio in the United States this year, prompting some members of Congress to inquire about the investment giant’s plans for the properties it now owns. Bisnow/Ethan Rothstein Brookfield purchased Yes Communities from GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, in the second quarter, public filings and statements from Brookfield management indicate. Brookfield hasn’t publicized its acquisition of the Denver-based operator of nearly 300 manufactured home developments, but three Democrats from the House of Representatives nonetheless sent a letter to the firm last month voicing concern about the purchase and seeking pledges for tenant protections. Reps. Maxwell Alejandro Frost, Gabe Vasquez and Rashida Tlaib asked management at New York-based Brookfield Asset Management, the publicly traded arm of Toronto-based Brookfield, and Brookfield Real Estate Group to provide assurances that residents’ quality of life wouldn’t be impacted by the deal. The representatives gave BAM until Nov. 20 to respond. The asset management giant hadn’t yet replied as of mid-November, Frost’s office confirmed to Bisnow on Nov. 9. Brookfield didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment. It hasn’t formally announced the acquisition, which was first rumored to be in the works in September 2025, but BAM said in second-quarter filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it acquired “the largest privately held U.S. manufactured home portfolio.” Yes Communities operates more than 55,000 housing sites across the U.S., with a focus on the Southwest, Midwest and Southeast. A purchase price for the portfolio is unknown, but BAM said it spent $5.2B in the second quarter on its real estate business, including the manufactured home portfolio and the take-private of an industrial outdoor storage portfolio. Brookfield announced a $1.2B all-cash deal in February to buy Peakstone Realty Trust, a REIT with 60 IOS properties and 16 traditional industrial assets. In its second-quarter filings, Brookfield Real Estate Income Trust disclosed a new investment in a 2% ownership interest in 294 manufactured housing properties at a book value of $86.6M, which aligns with the number of properties under the Yes Communities banner. BAM Chief Financial Officer Hadley Peer Marshall also disclosed on the second-quarter earnings call that a Brookfield fund had made its first investment by deploying capital to Yes Communities. Other affiliates of Brookfield may have also contributed capital for the Yes Communities acquisition. Brookfield REIT said in an investor presentation on its website that as of Sept. 30, it owned a 294-community manufactured housing portfolio across 23 states, the same number of states Yes Communities is active in. Wikimedia Commons; Office of Maxwell Frost Democratic Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Gabriel Vasquez and Maxwell Frost have asked Brookfield about its acquisition of Yes Communities. Executives from Brookfield held one virtual meeting with residents and their advocates following the acquisition that was facilitated by the Private Equity Stakeholder Project and MHAction, two nonprofit advocacy groups, PESP confirmed to Bisnow . GIC and another unnamed institutional investor acquired a 71% equity interest in Yes Communities in 2016, with Stockbridge Capital Group holding on to the remaining stake. Brookfield was reportedly in talks with GIC about acquiring its stake for more than $10B, and it is unclear exactly the size of Brookfield's interest in Yes Communities or how much it paid. In their letter from Oct. 13, the three members of Congress sought details about the acquisition. The letter outlines previous tenants' complaints with Yes Communities for high rent increases, excessive fees and neglect of routine maintenance and says that Brookfield “has the opportunity to change this scenario” and “support meaningful protections for its residents.” “Given the challenges our constituents have experienced at Yes! properties, as well as broader concerns about the private equity business model, we seek assurances that Brookfield will prioritize improving residents’ quality of life and protecting their economic and housing stability, rather than exacerbating the economic challenges they already face,” the representatives wrote. The letter specifically asks Brookfield to disclose whether it plans to increase rents by more than 3% annually, to outline its policy regarding new and existing fees, and to confirm whether it will refrain from serial eviction filings for routine rent collection. The letter asks BAM to commit to meet regularly with tenants and to cooperate with tenant groups that are seeking to collectively purchase their communities. Corporate ownership of single-family properties has for a decade been an issue in some political corners, but it spilled into the mainstream in recent years, including with the debate around the 21st Century Road to Housing Act and the focus on affordability from candidates in midterm races across the country. The housing legislation that made it to the president’s desk includes new restrictions on existing home purchases from institutional investors but carves out broad exemptions for new development of single-family communities built as rentals. items.title: Rapid absorption continues even as deliveries slow for the Phoenix multifamily market
items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Phoenix multifamily market report here.Highlights:Operating conditions in the Phoenix multifamily market improved during the third quarter, continuing patterns from the first half of this year. While property fundamentals have improved, investment activity has slowed in recent months.Vacancy dipped by 10 basis points in the third quarter, following steeper declines in the first half of the year. The current vacancy rate for stabilized properties is 6.5%, 70 basis points lower than levels from one year earlier.Area rents have gained ground in each of the first three quarters of 2026, although gains have been modest and current rents are still down slightly compared to one year ago. Rents ended the third quarter at $1,524 per month.Sales activity slowed in the third quarter, particularly among properties that have been delivered in recent years. The median price in sales that have closed to this point in 2026 is $229,600 per unit, while cap rates have averaged 6%.Phoenix multifamily market overviewThe Phoenix multifamily market has continued to record elevated levels of net absorption in 2026, which has combined with a slowing pace of new deliveries to support steady improvements in operating fundamentals. Vacancy remained 160 bps below its Q3 2025 peak of 28.0%, supported by occupancy gains in recently delivered buildings and declining sublease vacancy. Supply Raleigh-Durham’s life sciences overall vacancy rate increased a modest 10 basis points (bps) quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 26.4% in Q3, despite quarterly occupancy gains. The increase reflected the removal of the RTP/I-40 Corridor’s 201,056-square-foot (sf) Charles Sanders Center, previously subleased to the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, from the life sciences inventory following its lease to BASIS Independent Schools, removing it from the life sciences inventory. Vacancy remained 160 bps below its Q3 2025 peak of 28.0%, supported by occupancy gains in recently delivered buildings and declining sublease vacancy. Notably, sublease vacancy also improved by 70 bps year-over-year, falling from its record high of 3.6% in Q3 2025. Overall net absorption remained positive for the fourth consecutive quarter, bringing year-to-date (YTD) occupancy gains to more than 233,000 sf as tenant move-outs remained limited. Prior quarter leasing translated into Q3 move-ins, including Google Fiber occupying nearly 25,000 sf at Eastridge – Building 300 and Jazz Pharmaceuticals occupying more than 18,800 sf at TBC – Building 4020. Strong new leasing will continue to support occupancy gains, especially as large manufacturing users complete build outs of their spaces. Demand Nearly 130,000 sf of new leases were signed during Q3, bringing YTD activity to just under 397,000 sf. DG Matrix signed the quarter’s largest lease, taking nearly 55,000 sf at Southport 3 while diagnostics company Labcorp renewed for 33,500 sf at Eastridge – Building 100, contributing to nearly 64,000 sf of quarterly renewal activity. The RTP/I-40 Corridor submarket remained the primary driver of demand, representing 84.7% of new leasing YTD. Pricing Overall asking rates rose minimally QOQ, increasing by 0.3% to $38.63 per square foot (psf). Overall rates peaked at $40.31 psf in Q3 2023 when a wave of new, higher-priced space was introduced to the market. As premium space has leased, the market average has declined 4.2% from the peak. With construction paused and vacancy remaining elevated, asking rents are expected to remain relatively stable in the near term. items.description: October 2026 Hottest Housing Markets By Hannah Jones Nov 13, 2026 Highlights Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, Conn. claimed the top spot in October for the first time since a summer run on top from May – July 2026. Buyer demand remains highly concentrated in the hottest markets, where listings attracted 2.6 times the national average number of views per property. The Midwest and Northeast were the only regions represented in the Top 20 for the 37th consecutive month. The list was evenly split this month, with 10 markets in the Midwest and 10 in the Northeast. Homes in the hottest markets moved significantly faster than the national norm, with median time on market of 37 days, more than 3 weeks faster than the national norm. Among large U.S. metros, Jacksonville, FL posted the biggest year-over-year improvement, jumping 70 spots to rank 189th nationally. The Hartford, CT metro moved up one spot from last month to claim the top spot on the hottest housing markets list for the first time since the summer. Hartford has ranked in the top 20 a total of 57 times, but has claimed the top spot only eight times. Located in New England, midway between Boston and New York, Hartford is an ideal landing spot for homebuyers looking to take advantage of the relatively low home prices in an otherwise pricey part of the country. In October, Hartford attracted 4.1 times the national average number of viewers per property. Homes sold in just 37 days, one day slower than a year ago but almost a month faster than the national norm. At a median listing price of $440,000, Hartford is priced just above the national norm, in a region generally priced well-above. Realtor.com’s Market Hotness rankings take into account two aspects of the housing market: 1) market demand, as measured by unique views per property on Realtor.com, and 2) the pace of the market as measured by the number of days a listing remains active on Realtor.com. Springfield, Mass. and Rochester, N.Y. are priced below the national norm and well below the Northeast’s. New England’s compact geography is part of the draw. Hartford, New Haven, Waterbury and Springfield sit within roughly an hour’s drive of one another, so buyers can compare neighborhoods and price points across several metros without leaving the region. That flexibility concentrates demand, and inventory in these markets remains well below pre-pandemic norms. The pull shows up in buyer traffic, with all six New England markets on the list drawing at least 2.6 times the national average views per property, at or above the Top 20 average. For shoppers, widening the search within the region means more options but not much relief from competition, since the affordability that draws buyers to one market is drawing them to its neighbors as well. Most Improved Large Markets Large markets showed renewed momentum in October, moving up the list by 6 spots on average compared to last year. This suggests that big-city markets, while still trailing smaller and more affordable alternatives, are capturing renewed attention as buyers weigh the tradeoffs between affordability and access to larger job centers, especially as home prices soften across much of the country. Jacksonville, Fla. led all large markets with the biggest ranking improvement, climbing 70 spots year over year, while San Francisco and Denver posted notable gains of 38 and 33 spots respectively. Riverside jumped 32 spots, and Sacramento rounded out the top five most improved, advancing 31 spots. The biggest movers were still fairly low on the overall list, ranging from 73rd for San Francisco to 216th for Denver. Four of the five biggest movers were located in the West, with three in California and one in the South. Though the South and West remain outside the nation's hottest markets, some areas are beginning to show growing demand and faster time-on-market. San Francisco stands out, with homes selling more than 3 weeks faster than the national norm, an acceleration likely boosted by the area’s ongoing AI boom . items.title: The seasonal decline in housing inventory is in full force
items.description: Housing inventory Housing inventory has picked up recently, after mortgage rates went above 6.64% and then shot up toward 7.60%. Inventory growth had been very tame this year, with some weeks negative year over year. As housing inventory returns to normal levels, it takes weaker demand to get stronger growth and rates moving toward 7.60% did that. Still, it's more about sales taking longer to happen and demand being hit, because new listings data didn’t budge much recently. Now, we are in the full-blown seasonal decline as we get ready to prep for spring 2027. Inventory growth is running at 7.11% over last year even with easier comps, as last year demand was running toward a 9-month high in December of 2025. Weekly inventory change (Nov. 6-Nov. 13): Inventory fell from 902,740 to 895,988 Same week last year (Nov. 7-Nov. 14): Inventory fell from 842,257 to 836,487 New listings New listings have been in their seasonal decline since June and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since 2022. One concern I had about higher rates is that more people might simply not list their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 due to higher rates. However, that hasn’t happened; we did see a more noticeable year-over-year decline this last week, but for the most part it’s been a healthy year. In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years . Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years: 2026: 53,162 2025: 56,569 Price-cut percentage Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point demand fell and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%. In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indices show growth between 1% and 2%. However, with higher rates and a rising price-cut percentage, we will be closer to the forecast. Clearly, if rates hadn’t risen above 6.75%, pricing data wouldn’t have shown the recent slowdown. The price-cut percentage for last week: 2026: 43.% 2025: 42% 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% Last week wasn’t good for mortgage rates or the bond market: we had hawkish Fed statements and hot inflation data. We were getting closer to mortgage rates below 7% for the holidays, but they made a big reversal from 7.17% to 7.50%. In addition, President Trump talked about raising tariffs against Mexico and we still have no deal with Iran. Pretty much everything you needed for rates to go lower went the other way — something I talked about in this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they did improve last week. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% — spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility. However, we had a big reversal higher, and spreads improved some as the 10-year yield rose toward 5.14%. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads fell to 2.13% from 2.27% a week earlier. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle. If we had the best levels of spreads in 2026, mortgage rates would be 7.19% today, not 7.50% . If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.48% today, not 7.17% . Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. The key for the last four weeks: housing demand has stabilized, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, higher rates most likely will impact this week’s data more than last week, but the last four weeks have shown if we can get rates back below 7% and just have them stick, we can work with this. Housing demand typically grows when rates get below 6.64% and fades when rates are above 7%, especially if the move in rates is fast, like we saw recently. Still, it was encouraging to see stabilization in the data when rates were trying to get below 7% again. Of course, we are seeing big year-over-year declines in this data line as rates were heading toward 6% last year. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 50,623 2025: 60,722 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We did have 8% week-to-week growth last week as rates tried to get below 7% the week before. I expect the next purchase application data to get hit as rates picked up. This data was very positive year over year when rates were under 6.64%, but not so much when it headed toward 7% and got to 7.60%. items.title: How Training Veterans in Skilled Trades Could Speed Up Homebuilding and Ease Housing Costs
items.description: A severe shortage of skilled workers entering the residential construction sector has had a major impact on affordability, but the Home Builders Institute (HBI) believes the country’s large veteran population may be part of the solution. The skilled labor shortage has led to an increase in construction time, with each home taking nearly two months longer to build, according to an HBI study . Due to the delays, there was a reduction of 19,000 homes built in 2024, representing an economic loss of over $8 billion, the study found. Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) estimated that the construction industry needs to attract roughly 349,000 net new workers in 2026 and 456,000 new workers in 2027 to meet demand for construction services. There are a number of factors in the past 30 years that have led to the labor shortage, according to HBI CEO Ed Brady . First, a strong push for four-year degrees led many young people toward academic careers rather than trades. With more people retiring from the workforce than entering, the shortage began. The issue was compounded during the financial crisis of 2008, when the residential construction field lost tons of skilled workers because there wasn’t enough work. Without enough housing construction, workers left for jobs in manufacturing and hospitality or retired early, according to Brady. More recently, rocky immigration policies have challenged the skilled labor workforce, Brady explains. When finding a solution to the shortage became dire, HBI believed that the veteran and transitioning military population was “an untapped market.” The result was the HBI Military Services Program, which trains veterans, transitioning military service members, and their dependents in skilled trades. On Monday, HBI and Invitation Homes announced a new partnership that will continue HBI’s mission to create opportunities for transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families. The partnership includes an unspecified investment from Invitation Homes in HBI’s Military Services Program. It will also open doors for former military service members who complete HBI training to access job opportunities with the premier leasing and management company. For nearly a decade, HBI has been raising awareness of the benefits of a career in a skilled trade among former members. It has proceeded to train, certify, and assist veterans and their families in finding successful careers. HBI’s Military Services Program was supported early on by major companies like The Home Depot Foundation and Dewalt. It was recently given a $1 million gift from Google.org , and now Invitation Homes has joined the worthy cause. These vital investments help HBI reach even more service members on their mission, according to Brady. “It provides scale. We’re not changing our model—we feel like our model works.
